title: Small and medium enterprises - Wikipedia
content: Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) or small and medium businesses (SMBs), also sometimes grouped as small, medium, and micro enterprises (SMMEs), are businesses whose personnel and revenue numbers fall below certain limits. The abbreviation "SME" is used by many national agencies and international organizations, such as the World Bank, the OECD, the European Union, the United Nations, and the World Trade Organization (WTO). [...] SMEs are a crucial element in the supplier network of large enterprises which are already on their way towards Industry 4.0. According to German economist Hans-Heinrich Bass, "empirical research on SME as well as policies to promote SME have a long tradition in [[West] Germany]( "West Germany"), dating back into the 19th century. Until the mid-20th century, most researchers considered SME as an impediment to further economic development and SME policies were thus designed in the framework of [...] Developing countries tend to have a higher proportion of small and medium-sized enterprises. SMEs are also responsible for driving innovation and competition "Competition (economics)") in many economic sectors. Although they create more new jobs than large firms, SMEs also account for the majority of job destruction and contraction.

title: Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs) - Definition, Importance
content:
In order to be successful, SMEs focus on creating new products or services; hence, they are capable of adapting faster to the changing requirements of the market. SMEs play a vital role in shaping a country’s economy. They can be considered an attractive and huge innovative system. Due to the socially and economically beneficial effects of the SMEs, the sector is considered an area of strategic interest in an economy.

### 2. Creates a more competitive and healthier economy [...] The U.S. also has a specific definition of SMEs based on the industry they operate in. For example, if a company is in the manufacturing industry, it can be classified as an SME if it has a maximum of 500 employees, but a company in wholesale trade can have only 100. Differences also exist within an industry’s sectors. [...] The traits include annual sales, number of employees, the number of assets owned by the company, market capitalization, or any combination of these features. The United States also defines SMEs differently from one industry to another.

title: What Are Small and Midsize Enterprises (SMEs)? | The Motley Fool
content: SMEs are businesses whose size falls below a certain threshold. Limits vary by country and industry. [...] SMEs might be smaller than large multinational corporations, but they're mighty. They are the backbone of the economy. In the U.S., there are more than 30 million SMEs -- 99.9% of all businesses, according to the SBA. SMEs account for almost half the U.S. workforce (47.1%), and they've created two-thirds of all net new private sector jobs over the past few decades. [...] For example, the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) has set size standards of revenue or number of employees for every industry to determine if a company qualifies as a small business. In agriculture, a soybean farmer pulling in $2.25 million or less in revenue qualifies as a small business, but the standard climbs to $19 million for chicken egg production. title: SME definition - Internal Market, Industry, Entrepreneurship and SMEs
content:
Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) represent 99% of all businesses. The definition of an SME is crucial for access to finance and EU support programmes. However, when SMEs grow beyond a certain size, they often face a significant increase in compliance obligations, which can create a ‘cliff-edge’ effect that discourages growth and limits competitiveness. These ceilings apply to the figures for individual firms only. A firm that is part of a larger group may need to include staff headcount/turnover/balance sheet data from that group too.

title: What Are Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs)? | Salesforce
content:
SME Overview:

## What Defines a Small and Medium Enterprises (SME)?

The term small and medium enterprises (SME) is a broad classification that generally centers on employee count and annual revenue. These benchmarks vary a lot by country and sector, but they establish the size where a business moves beyond “startup” status and begins to face more complex operational challenges, similar to those of large enterprises. [...] To achieve sustainable growth, leaders in the SME segment focus on implementing smart strategies and adopting scalable technology. This approach allows a business to simplify operations, deliver exceptional customer experiences, and make swift, data-informed decisions that fuel revenue and profitability. Understanding the specific needs of an SME is the first step toward building the right operational foundation for long-term success.

SME Overview: [...] Share the story

The journey from a small and medium business (SMB) to a thriving midsize enterprise isn't a simple one. It involves navigating a complex series of growth stages, and companies that successfully make this transition — often called small and medium enterprises (SMEs) — must constantly balance ambition with efficiency. They're large enough to compete with major corporations but still operate with limited resources and a high demand for agility.

title: SMEs Finance | World Bank Group
content:
Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) are the backbone of most economies, representing around 90 percent of all businesses and accounting for more than half of global employment. In developing countries, SMEs are central to economic diversification, productivity, and poverty reduction. Yet, they face persistent challenges in obtaining the financing needed to start, sustain, and grow. [...] Beyond income, access to finance unlocks opportunity. It enables entrepreneurs to innovate, expand, and hire, empowering women and youth and strengthening communities. Women tend to reinvest much of their earnings into their families and local economies, creating a powerful multiplier effect. Supporting SMEs—especially women-owned and youth-led enterprises—is thus central to building inclusive and sustainable growth.
